{"id": "10:31/q01", "question": "What is rizq, and why is God called the Provider?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q01/p1", "position": "Rizq is a continuing usable gift or benefit; God alone is the Provider because He creates it.", "reasons": "Jishumi says the recipient may use it and others cannot withhold it; the divine title is exclusive as Lord is, despite ordinary possessive usage. Qushayri grounds God's provision in His sole creation."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q02", "question": "What provision comes from heaven and earth?", "turns_on": "Whether sky and earth name rain and vegetation, wider causes, spiritual gifts, or their inhabitants.", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q02/p1", "position": "Rain comes from heaven and plants or crops from earth.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas and the commentators in Wahidi, and Bg and Ts in Study Quran, give this pairing. Razi says animal diets ultimately depend on plants, since endless animal consumption is impossible; Ibn Kathir cites 80:27–31 and 67:21 for the rain-fed produce. Ibn Ashur includes grain, fruit and pasture. Abu Hayyan calls these essential to life and a gift from upper and lower worlds. Muqatil, Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya and others join the pairing to the larger proof."}, {"id": "10:31/q02/p2", "position": "The provision covers the full range of heavenly and earthly causes and benefits.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports al-Asamm's clouds, rain, celestial bodies and vegetation. Biqai adds other sky benefits and other means of life from earth. Alusi names rain and sun above and materials below, the earth receiving what heaven supplies. Kuranyolu adds warmth, resources and habitats, and says sustenance matters because other resources help only while life continues. Kashshaf calls it God's abundant favor and widened mercy; Baydawi permits both sources to be taken broadly."}, {"id": "10:31/q02/p3", "position": "Provision also includes bodily and spiritual gifts.", "reasons": "Qushayri distinguishes bodily obedience or failure from spiritual connection, heedlessness, punishment or respite; for spirits he names realities of intimacy as provision. Asad connects physical and spiritual sustenance with heaven, earth, hearing and sight; Study Quran reports this from Q."}, {"id": "10:31/q02/p4", "position": "Provision may be understood as coming from inhabitants of heaven and earth, with a noun omitted.", "reasons": "Baydawi proposes the inhabitants as a reading with ellipsis; Samin and Alusi explain the required omitted ahl or possessive construction."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q03", "question": "What does min in 'from heaven and earth' express?", "turns_on": "Whether min directly marks origin or depends on an omitted expression for inhabitants.", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q03/p1", "position": "It marks the source of provision.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says min indicates the origin of the essential provision and the generosity of both worlds. Samin and Alusi allow this straightforward construction; Alusi sees no need to change it."}, {"id": "10:31/q03/p2", "position": "It may be partitive, with an implied possessive referring to the inhabitants.", "reasons": "Samin requires omitted ahl; Alusi describes an implicit idafa. Alusi objects that the verse does not explicitly place God among the inhabitants of heaven and earth."}, {"id": "10:31/q03/p3", "position": "It may explain a kind, after an omitted word for inhabitants or provisions.", "reasons": "Samin says the reading of kind needs omitted ahl; Alusi describes an explanatory min after an ellipsis."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q04", "question": "How does am introduce the question about hearing and sight?", "turns_on": "The grammatical status of man and whether am is disconnected, with the shared rhetorical effect of moving to a new proof.", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q04/p1", "position": "It transfers the argument to another question without cancelling the first.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan requires an interrogative hamza for am to amount to bal plus interrogation. Samin calls it a Qur'anic transfer rather than cancellation; Alusi and Ibn Ashur likewise treat it as transition."}, {"id": "10:31/q04/p2", "position": "It is disconnected am meaning bal alone, followed by the explicit interrogative man.", "reasons": "Samin says neither a preceding interrogative hamza nor equivalence licenses connected am; compare 27:84. He still describes the rhetorical move as a transfer."}, {"id": "10:31/q04/p3", "position": "Am can precede man because man is not inherently interrogative and stands for the interrogative alif.", "reasons": "Akhfash says am supplies an indispensable sense. He extends the explanation to am after hal: interrogation originally belongs to alif, and a cited poem has hal ... am hal."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q05", "question": "What does God's ownership of hearing and sight mean?", "turns_on": "Whether ownership specifies creation, protection, ongoing control, or a spiritual capacity; Abu Hayyan disputes how much the wording alone specifies.", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q05/p1", "position": "He creates, forms, and gives these faculties.", "reasons": "Wahidi, Qurtubi and others take ownership as creation or gift. Kashshaf, Baydawi and Nasafi stress their remarkable formation. Alusi prefers creation because the sequence joins creative power to provision, citing 35:3; Ibn Kathir compares 67:23 and 6:46, and Study Quran 46:26, 23:78, 32:9 and 67:23. Ibn Ashur calls them subtle and useful. Abu Hayyan reports Zamakhshari's creation gloss but cautions that its detail is not entailed by the words."}, {"id": "10:31/q05/p2", "position": "He protects these delicate organs from harm.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi and Alusi mention their vulnerability to frequent injury. Abu Hayyan reports this from Zamakhshari but says that such a nuance does not follow from the wording."}, {"id": "10:31/q05/p3", "position": "He governs their operation and can strengthen, preserve, or remove them.", "reasons": "Tabari and Ibn Kathir say God can take them away; Jishumi reports Abu Muslim's granting and removal. Abu Hayyan says hearing enables perception and sight surveys creation, and that both stand for the senses generally as the noblest. Elmalili calls them means of using provision. Tabatabai and Kuranyolu say sensory equipment lets people benefit from provision; without it they would perish. Kuranyolu says the senses work under divine laws. Abu Hayyan resists reading more specific creative or protective details from the wording."}, {"id": "10:31/q05/p4", "position": "He enables reception of admonition and lessons, and spiritual sight or blindness.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports Abu Muslim's moral interpretation. Qushayri says monotheism perfects some people's sight while others are blinded to realization. Elmalili connects the senses with recognizing truth, certainty and external reality, citing 3:18, 6:103 and 17:85; he says true perception is a divine act and invokes the sacred hadith of God becoming a devoted servant's hearing."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q06", "question": "Why is hearing singular but sights plural?", "turns_on": "Whether the contrast is chiefly in the diversity of perceptions or in the nouns' forms and reference.", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q06/p1", "position": "Hearing is shared or uniform, while seeing is more diverse.", "reasons": "Biqai says most people share hearing equally; Elmalili says seeing is more various or numerous. Suyuti says sound is one kind whereas sight takes diverse colors and forms."}, {"id": "10:31/q06/p2", "position": "Hearing is a collective verbal noun, while plural sights makes universal reference explicit.", "reasons": "Suyuti calls hearing verbal-noun-like but sight an organ name. Ibn Ashur says singular hearing denotes the species, whereas singular sight could be mistaken for one individual's sight; he contrasts 17:36 and cites 6:46."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q07", "question": "How does God bring the living from the dead and the dead from the living?", "turns_on": "The scope of life and death: biological generation, simple animation, faith, knowledge, or the broader human and functional sense; Razi and Alusi favor biological examples, Tabatabai the broader contextual one.", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q07/p1", "position": "Living beings and plants arise from nonliving matter or reproductive material, which in turn comes from living things.", "reasons": "Muqatil names human life from semen. Wahidi lists plant from earth, human from sperm, bird from egg, stalk from grain and palm from seed, plus reverses. Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Razi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Biqai and Ibn Ashur add drops, eggs, seeds, embryos, chicks and crops. Razi says most favor this as nearer the literal sense; Alusi prefers the animal/drop reading. Ibn Ashur says definite nouns denote species. Elmalili adds organic life from food and inorganic matter; he argues changes between opposed natures reveal power beyond regular nature. Ibn Kathir holds the general wording includes all earlier interpretations. Study Quran points to 30:19 and 6:95."}, {"id": "10:31/q07/p2", "position": "God gives life and death or reverses living and lifeless states generally.", "reasons": "Jishumi and Baydawi state the direct life/death reading. Ibn Kathir says the verse's generality embraces the interpretations, while Kuranyolu says living beings emerge from lifeless things and become lifeless."}, {"id": "10:31/q07/p3", "position": "A believer arises from an unbeliever and an unbeliever from a believer.", "reasons": "Qushayri gives this interpretation; Wahidi, Qurtubi, Razi, Nasafi and Alusi include it. Razi says most prefer the literal reproductive example instead; Alusi likewise prefers that first explanation."}, {"id": "10:31/q07/p4", "position": "The contrast can encompass scholars from their opposites and other spiritual reversals.", "reasons": "Nasafi explicitly adds scholars to animals, chicks, crops and believers emerging from their opposites; Tabatabai connects human life with re

ason and religion in this context."}, {"id": "10:31/q07/p5", "position": "In context it is the emergence of reasonable, religious human life from its opposite.", "reasons": "Tabatabai argues the sequence progresses from human sustenance through human senses to human life. He favors the broad functional sense of productive life arising from an unproductive source and the reverse, over a merely biological restriction."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q08", "question": "What counts as life and death in this expression?", "turns_on": "Whether life is restricted to organismal vitality or extends to any fitting, productive effect.", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q08/p1", "position": "Life first denotes the principle of knowledge and power in animals and also includes vital processes in plants.", "reasons": "Tabatabai starts with animal life and extends the inquiry to plants; he reports narrower accounts of animals alone or animals and plants emerging from nonliving matter, with dead parts separated from living organisms."}, {"id": "10:31/q08/p2", "position": "Life more broadly means capacity to produce fitting effects, and death its absence.", "reasons": "Tabatabai applies this to earth, actions, speech and human beings; religion is called life because true Islam is the divinely created human nature. He prefers this functional sense in the verse's context: beneficial life from an unproductive source and conversely."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q09", "question": "Why is the emergence of living from dead and dead from living phrased this way?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q09/p1", "position": "The reversal of opposites displays divine power and heightens wonder.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan calls it the production of opposites from one another. Biqai sees a move from deficiency to completion. Ibn Ashur calls the reciprocal wording a riddle and antithesis, with no hidden allusion such as one might find in 3:27. Elmalili reasons that opposed transformations reveal active power beyond nature."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q10", "question": "How is al-mayyit read in both occurrences?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q10/p1", "position": "The light form mayt drops gemination of ya, including the accusative mayta.", "reasons": "Qiraat-ER records the reduction in both forms; some grammarians distinguish mayt as already dead from mayyit as dying or recently dead."}, {"id": "10:31/q10/p2", "position": "The forms of al-mayyit are read with a doubled yāʾ.", "reasons": "Nashr reports Abū Jaʿfar doubling the yāʾ in the listed forms of الميتة/ميتا, بلد ميت, and الحي من الميت والميت من الحي."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q11", "question": "What does managing the affair include?", "turns_on": "Whether the question asks for the ultimate source of governance or permits a subordinate cosmic manager.", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q11/p1", "position": "God alone determines and carries out the affairs of all creation.", "reasons": "Mujahid says He decides and executes; Tabari includes heaven, earth, what is in them and people; Wahidi includes this world and the next. Jishumi names day, night, seasons, life and death. Razi adds upper and lower worlds and spirits and bodies. Ibn Kathir says no one can overturn His judgment and cites 55:29 for creatures' dependence. Ibn Atiyya says this governance rests on complete eternal knowledge, without thought or change. Elmalili stresses ordering the universe by command; Tabatabai says all delegated-seeming management ultimately ends with God."}, {"id": "10:31/q11/p2", "position": "God initiates and continually renews the changing turns of cosmic affairs.", "reasons": "Sulami reports this from an unnamed source and from al-Wasiti; al-Wasiti says it defeats claims of independent agency based on one's own acts and work."}, {"id": "10:31/q11/p3", "position": "A cosmic pole may manage the world and hold up the sky by God's permission.", "reasons": "Alusi reports some mystics appealing to 79:5 for a nondivine manager; some claim the pole and God differ only in consideration because of the pole's perfect nearness. Critics call this unity of being, rejected by most theologians and some Sufis including al-Imam al-Rabbani. Alusi argues that comparison with angels or Jesus acting by permission fails because the question asks for the ultimate source."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q12", "question": "Why does the question about managing the affair follow the specific signs?", "turns_on": "Whether the coordination is described chiefly as generalization after specifics or as emphatic joining of related expressions.", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q12/p1", "position": "It generalizes from particular powers to God's unlimited governance.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Razi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Biqai, Alusi and Ibn Ashur describe this widening. Alusi says all affairs originate with God and return to Him though humans cannot know their details; Ibn Ashur compares 51:21–22. Suyuti says naming a particular first emphasizes it, and rejects denial of the general-after-particular construction. Study Quran points to 10:3."}, {"id": "10:31/q12/p2", "position": "The coordinated expressions can also serve emphasis through conjunction of near synonyms.", "reasons": "Burhan reports Zamakhshari grouping the governance question with the provision question as coordinated expressions. Burhan says waw can join synonyms or near synonyms to intensify a statement, particularly differently worded pairs, and cites 3:146, 20:112, 20:77, 74:22, 12:86, 74:28, 4:171, 20:107, 43:80, 5:48, 17:52, 33:67, 33:12 and 35:35."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q13", "question": "Who answers 'Allah,' and why?", "turns_on": "Whether the forecast is restricted to the actual polytheist audience or also states what any thoughtful person must recognize.", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q13/p1", "position": "The polytheists, particularly the Meccans or Quraysh, admit God performs these acts.", "reasons": "Muqatil names Quraysh; Razi, Ibn Atiyya, Ibn Kathir, Biqai, Alusi, Tabatabai and others say the admission is unavoidable or immediate because the signs are plain. Qushayri says their words are conjecture without inward conviction. Razi says they sought idols' nearness or intercession while knowing idols cannot help or harm. Asad says they assigned divine or semidivine qualities to intermediaries (7:172); Islahi adds supposed favored delegates with powers over sustenance and children. Study Quran reports R's comparison to 29:61, 29:63, 31:25, 39:38, 43:87, 39:3 and 10:18 and says many saw Allah as head of a pantheon."}, {"id": "10:31/q13/p2", "position": "Any honest and reflective rational person would answer God, even if the polytheists did not.", "reasons": "Qurtubi says creation of heaven and earth is near self-evident to reason; if the idolaters deny the premise, the proof still reaches a thoughtful person."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q14", "question": "How does the first fa connect the command to ask with their answer?", "turns_on": "Whether the condition is inherent in the command or supplied in the grammar.", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q14/p1", "position": "The command to ask itself functions as a condition: if he asks, they will answer.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur compares 17:51–52; without the command-as-condition sense, the fa would be absent, as in 23:84–85. He says supplying an explicit conditional is close in meaning but differs as a grammatical rather than semantic estimate."}, {"id": "10:31/q14/p2", "position": "An implied conditional can be supplied before the answer.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reports this from grammarians and compares command constructions in 14:31 and 17:53; he sees little difference in sense from treating the command itself as conditional."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q15", "question": "What is the syntax of Allah in their answer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q15/p1", "position": "Allah is the subject of an omitted predicate: God alone performs these acts.", "reasons": "Alusi gives the ellipsis and says the polytheists reply without hesitation because the evidence cannot be denied."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q16", "question": "What does the final question ask them to do?", "turns_on": "Whether taqwa is a rebuke calling for fear and abandonment of shirk, a call to heed the warning, a specific practice, or a question about ability.", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q16/p1", "position": "Fear God's punishment and abandon associating partners with Him.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Tabari, Wahidi, Jishumi, Baghawi, Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, Razi, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, Biqai and others derive this from their admission that only God performs the acts. Qurtubi includes retribution here and hereafter. Alusi says the interrogative rebukes their actual failure and implies 'you know this, yet do not fear.' Study Quran reports Z linking it to their error and coming punishment, with 7:65, 23:23, 23:32, 23:87 and 26:11. Islahi adds fear of false attributions and denial of God's attributes."}, {"id": "10:31/q16/p2", "position": "Take warning and stop.", "reasons": "Ibn Jawzi reports this from Ibn Abbas; Abu Hayyan offers it as an alternative to fearing punishment."}, {"id": "10:31/q16/p3", "position": "Guard against Hell through the five daily prayers.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim reports this specific gloss from al-Dahhak."}, {"id": "10:31/q16/p4", "position": "The question may ask whether they are able to fear God.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim reports the alternative gloss from Mujahid."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q17", "question": "How are the fa and omitted object in the final rebuke understood?", "turns_on": "Whether the omitted complement is a single object, as Alusi insists, or the analysis implies two.", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q17/p1", "position": "The fa draws the rebuke from their admission, with a further explanatory fa and an understood object of fear.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says 'then say' follows their answer and the last fa draws its consequence. He takes God as the unspoken object; Alusi takes God's

Alusi rejects the implication in al-Qadi's analysis that tattaqun governs two objects."}, {"id": "10:31/q17/p2", "position": "The construction might imply that tattaqun governs two objects.", "reasons": "Alusi ascribes this apparent implication to al-Qadi but rejects it: here the verb governs one omitted object."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q18", "question": "What overall proof do the verse's questions establish?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q18/p1", "position": "Their acknowledged dependence on God's exclusive powers proves His sole lordship and right to worship, and rebukes shirk.", "reasons": "Zajjaj says only God can provide, make senses and life, and govern. Ibn Atiyya calls the proof inescapable; Qurtubi says reason recognizes a creator even if idolaters resist. Razi says the argument follows an exposure of idolatry; Abu Hayyan calls its evidence undeniable. Biqai and Jishumi also find a proof of resurrection. Tabatabai says it meets idolaters' belief in separately managed domains and proves all management ends with God, which entails exclusive worship. Asad says intermediaries empty belief in one God of spiritual value. Islahi says the admitted creator and giver of life must be sole Lord, defeating denial of resurrection too. Study Quran's introduction adds false gods cannot create or guide."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q19", "question": "Why do the proofs proceed in this order?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q19/p1", "position": "They move from human needs and familiar gifts to the origin of life and then universal management.", "reasons": "Biqai says the questions first invoke experienced gifts and then prior creation. Tabatabai says rain and plants sustain people, senses let them benefit, and life follows in the sequence. He describes three ordered proofs: one against idolaters' scheme of management, then afterlife accountability, then truth for the spiritual elect; he says reversing that order would miss the intended audience. Samarrai urges reading language in its actual setting."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q20", "question": "What does the verse imply about predestination, human acts, and divine provision?", "turns_on": "Whether exclusive divine creation and provision determine all acts or leave independent human acts and sources of sustenance.", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q20/p1", "position": "All created events remain under God's settled will, decree, and power; causes cannot reverse His decree.", "reasons": "Qushayri says the decree has already passed, all creatures and events are subject to it, and created causes cannot change what is eternal. He rejects both assigning creation-partners within predestination and denying resurrection as unbelief. Sulami's report from al-Wasiti says ongoing divine management leaves no independent agency based on human works."}, {"id": "10:31/q20/p2", "position": "People themselves perform idol worship and fabrication and are rightly punished for them.", "reasons": "Jishumi argues this against the Compulsionists' account of human acts; the reproach and punishment assume accountable human action."}, {"id": "10:31/q20/p3", "position": "God's provision includes forbidden as well as lawful sustenance.", "reasons": "Alusi reports Sahib al-Intisaf's use of the verse against the Qadariyyah claim that God supplies only lawful sustenance and humans supply themselves with forbidden sustenance; he calls that hidden associationism."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q21", "question": "How do the surrounding verses prepare or extend this challenge?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q21/p1", "position": "The preceding exposure of idols, their helplessness, and their worshippers' accountability prepares this challenge.", "reasons": "Jishumi says idols and worshippers are gathered then separated and disavow one another; even animated idols cannot help, harm, avert punishment or intercede independently, and each person receives the consequence of good or evil. Abu Ja'far in Samarrai says earlier questions about provision and the senses have already awakened the audience, leaving the punishment reminder. Samarrai emphasizes setting and context."}, {"id": "10:31/q21/p2", "position": "The provision and life questions connect with other verses explaining the same signs.", "reasons": "Ibn Jawzi refers life from death to 3:27; Ibn Ashur compares 3:27 but says this passage has no hidden allusion. Study Quran points from the life question to 30:19 and 6:95 and from governance to 10:3. Ibn Kathir invokes 80:27–31, 67:21, 67:23, 6:46 and 55:29 for produce, senses and divine dependence."}, {"id": "10:31/q21/p3", "position": "The adjoining discussion of truth contrasts sure knowledge of God with conjecture and spiritual blindness.", "reasons": "Qushayri says Truth is a divine name, God possesses and actualizes truth, and human truth is good action, sound belief and permissible speech. Conjecture is a preference without certainty; it is defective about God, while certainty about one's own unseen future is also defective. He cites 12:108 for calling with insight and says hearing the Qur'an increases some people's blindness but guides the spiritually realized. The verse's answer itself, he says, may be mere words without inner conviction."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q22", "question": "What report illustrates the marvel of the created senses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q22/p1", "position": "Ali praised God for sight through fat or fluid, hearing through bone, and speech through flesh.", "reasons": "Razi, Abu Hayyan, Biqai and Kuranyolu relay the same saying; Kuranyolu renders the sight medium as fluid, the others as fat. The wording varies slightly while the three faculties are the same."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q23", "question": "Does the old polytheist argument have a modern counterpart?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q23/p1", "position": "Modern idolaters repeat the same pattern despite describing their practices as monotheistic.", "reasons": "Islahi equates their claimed mediation with the Arabs' treatment of favored creatures as delegated powers and intercessors."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q24", "question": "How does the wording for bringing out the dead here differ from the parallel in al-Anʿām?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q24/p1", "position": "This verse uses the verbal form, whereas the parallel in al-Anʿām uses the nominal form مخرج الميت.", "reasons": "Burhan contrasts the nominal مخرج الميت in al-Anʿām with the verbal يخرج in this parallel passage."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q25", "question": "Why is heaven singular in the provision question?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q25/p1", "position": "The singular expresses heaven as a generic class where the context does not require a plural.", "reasons": "Burhan says the singular form names the generic class when context does not call for the plural."}]}
{"id": "10:31/q26", "question": "What is the effect of using one shared expression for heaven and earth?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:31/q26/p1", "position": "A single shared expression presents the general class and foregrounds the main purpose; repeating the relative and locative phrase specifies individuals.", "reasons": "Samarrai-Asrar reports an unnamed scholar's distinction between a single relative expression and repeated relative and locative expressions, mentioning 2:255 and al-Raḥmān."}]}
{"id": "10:32/q01", "question": "Whom does 'that is Allah, your true Lord' identify, and on what grounds?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:32/q01/p1", "position": "The one whose creative, life-giving, providing and governing acts the audience acknowledged is Allah, their true Lord, alone entitled to worship.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj and Ibn Abbas in Wahidi ground the identification in the preceding admission and deny the partners any such powers. Tabari and Ibn Kathir draw exclusive worship from the audience's own acknowledgment. Baydawi lists creation, enlivening, provision and governance; Biqai says true lordship requires all the listed attributes. Razi adds certain sovereignty and mercy; Nasafi says careful reasoning makes lordship certain. Elmalili includes creation, command, mastery and authority; Asad excludes even a slight share of divinity. Ibn Ashur says the initial fa draws the conclusion from 10:31, the demonstrative gathers the qualities, and naming Allah exposes the polytheists' error. Study Quran connects it to 10:31 and, with 6:95 and 6:102, says reflection removes doubt. Islahi calls the demonstrative the logical consequence of the acknowledged attributes. Jishumi takes the preceding questions to establish both unity and resurrection through rain, plants, clouds, celestial bodies and vegetation (the latter list from al-Asamm)."}]}
{"id": "10:32/q02", "question": "How is 'that is Allah, your true Lord, the Truth' parsed?", "turns_on": "The notes offer different grammatical analyses of the divine name, 'your Lord', and al-haqq.", "positions": [{"id": "10:32/q02/p1", "position": "The word al-haqq admits the same three accusative analyses as in verse 10:30.", "reasons": "Al-Farra invokes the three earlier analyses; al-Nahhas explicitly points to 10:30."}, {"id": "10:32/q02/p2", "position": "Allah may qualify the demonstrative and rabbukum be its predicate, or Allah may be the predicate and rabbukum an apposition; al-haqq qualifies or further predicates lordship.", "reasons": "Alusi gives these alternative nominal analyses and notes that the demonstrative sums the acknowledged qualities."}]}

epend on a creator and may perish.", "reasons": "Al-Khattabi, reported by Ibn al-Jawzi, defines the Real as established and valid in existence. {"id": "10:32/q04", "question": "What is the truth and error contrasted in 'what after truth except error'?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish worship from its objects, and the verse's specific polemic from a general truth/error principle.", "positions": [{"id": "10:32/q04/p1", "position": "Truth is worship of God alone, and error is abandoning it for worship of Satan, idols or any rival; association makes worship unacceptable.", "reasons": "Muqatil in Wahidi calls the alternative worship of Satan; Ibn Abbas in Wahidi names their adopted gods. Tabari, Baghawi, Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Ibn Kathir, Alusi, Ibn Ashur and Tabatabai apply the contrast to exclusive divine worship. Alusi says associated worship is not accepted. Wahidi and Baydawi stress that rivals cannot provide, enliven or cause death. Ibn Atiyya praises the Quran's concise clarity."}, {"id": "10:32/q04/p2", "position": "Truth is the true Lord Himself, and error is the supposed gods that possess none of His powers.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas in Wahidi names the adopted gods; Alusi explicitly reports this construal as an alternative to the worship-focused construal. Qurtubi cites 31:30, where God is Truth and invoked rivals are false."}, {"id": "10:32/q04/p3", "position": "Truth and error are opposites with no middle ground: leaving manifest truth entails error, shirk and misery.", "reasons": "Jishumi says no third rank exists; Kashshaf adds shirk and misery. Razi argues contradictory propositions cannot both be true or false. Qurtubi compares the truth/falsehood contrast and 31:30. Abu Hayyan calls the question a negative assertion and rebuke. Ibn Ashur explains 'after' as 'other than' when truth is absent; Tabatabai sees paired truth/guidance and falsehood/error; Elmalili applies this to every creed other than monotheism. Tabatabai elsewhere says unified truths cohere, whereas falsehood is scattered and divisive."}, {"id": "10:32/q04/p4", "position": "The contrast can broadly include monotheism and worship beyond the specific opposition of God and idols.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this expanded construal alongside the two narrower construals."}]}
{"id": "10:32/q05", "question": "Does this truth/error contrast extend to disputed acts and legal rulings?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse's contrast is restricted by its context of belief and worship or also covers legal deeds.", "positions": [{"id": "10:32/q05/p1", "position": "Here the no-middle principle governs foundational belief and unbelief, especially God's oneness; derivative legal rulings can have ambiguity and differing laws.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi cite 5:48 and the Prophetic distinction between clear lawful, clear forbidden and doubtful matters. Qurtubi says deeds are not the primary subject; Abu Hayyan rejects using this passage as proof that chess is error because laws and jurists differ. Qurtubi favors this reading from the preceding proof of God's acts and exclusive right to worship."}, {"id": "10:32/q05/p2", "position": "The truth/error principle can judge conduct: what God forbids is error and what He permits is guidance.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports this broader reading, based on God alone permitting and forbidding, but rejects it in favor of the context about worship. Malik also applies the verse to an unspecified disputed matter and to games; those applications are detailed below."}]}
{"id": "10:32/q06", "question": "What does al-dalal mean in Arabic and religious usage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:32/q06/p1", "position": "It means straying from a straight route or losing something; religious usage especially applies it to unsound belief, while context can also mean lack of knowledge.", "reasons": "Ibn Arafa gives deviation and loss. Qurtubi derives the sense from leaving a road's direction and says 93:7 may mean the Prophet was unaware of scripture and faith before guidance, as 42:52 indicates, rather than unbelieving."}]}
{"id": "10:32/q07", "question": "How does ma-dha and the exception in 'what after truth except error' work?", "turns_on": "Whether dha merges with ma as one interrogative or functions as a relative pronoun.", "positions": [{"id": "10:32/q07/p1", "position": "Ma and dha form one emphatic interrogative 'what'; the question works as a negation, permitting illa.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan gives 'after truth' as predicate. Al-Samin says interrogative force predominates over the demonstrative. Ibn Ashur says the combination often adds emphasis, citing 2:26 and 10:50 for other uses."}, {"id": "10:32/q07/p2", "position": "Dha is a relative pronoun meaning 'that which', with its clause predicated of interrogative ma; the rhetorical negation still takes illa.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Samin report this alternate grammatical construction. Ibn Ashur allows relative dha elsewhere but favors the emphatic combination here."}]}
{"id": "10:32/q08", "question": "Why are the question and its opening fa phrased this way?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:32/q08/p1", "position": "The fa draws a reproachful inference from proof of God's lordship, and the question emphatically denies any alternative to truth.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur explains the inferential fa; Abu Hayyan and al-Samin say an interrogative supplies a negative assertion with illa. Ibn Ashur takes 'after' as 'other than what follows when truth is absent.'"}]}
{"id": "10:32/q09", "question": "How is the truth/error contrast expressed concisely?", "turns_on": "Whether the paired implication should be described directly or as a formal two-sided omission.", "positions": [{"id": "10:32/q09/p1", "position": "The wording pairs truth with guidance and, by implication, falsehood with error.", "reasons": "Tabatabai prefers this direct account of the compressed opposites and rejects the more technical account. {"id": "10:32/q10", "question": "What does 'how are you turned away?' ask?", "turns_on": "The Arabic interrogative is explained as 'how' or as a metaphorical 'where are you going?'", "positions": [{"id": "10:32/q10/p1", "position": "It asks how they can turn from acknowledged truth, guidance and God's worship to error, idols or beings unable to provide, enliven or kill.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas glosses the interrogative as 'how' and, in Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi, asks how reason could choose powerless beings. Ibn Ashur treats the path as a metaphor for reasoning. Tabatabai asks how long such turning continues; Asad gives the literal question."}, {"id": "10:32/q10/p2", "position": "It asks where they are going or straying, even without a literal person turning them.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim in Jishumi makes the nonliteral point. Ibn Atiyya compares the reproach to 'where are you going?' in 81:26; Elmalili also asks where they are being led."}]}
{"id": "10:32/q11", "question": "What force does the closing question carry?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:32/q11/p1", "position": "It rebukes and expresses astonishment at their actual turning from truth, with a further inferential fa.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya calls it reproach; Alusi says the interrogative expresses astonishment and denial of their real action, stronger than merely denying occurrence. {"id": "10:32/q12", "question": "Who causes the turning described by the passive verb?", "turns_on": "Whether humans create their turning or God acts while they remain blameworthy for its cause.", "positions": [{"id": "10:32/q12/p1", "position": "The people turn themselves: God cannot reproach unbelievers for a turning He compelled.", "reasons": "Al-Jubbai in Razi and Abu Hayyan argues from the verse's blame, comparing a blind person who would not claim to blind himself. Jishumi argues that idol worship and false claims are human acts deserving punishment, against the Compulsionists."}, {"id": "10:32/q12/p2", "position": "God is the agent of the act, while the rebuke concerns its blameworthy cause rather than expressing surprise at God's own act.", "reasons": "Alusi states this as his doctrinal solution to the passive question."}]}
{"id": "10:32/q13", "question": "How does the next decree relate to this verse?", "turns_on": "Which preceding element grounds the decree and how divine predetermination is understood.", "positions": [{"id": "10:32/q13/p1", "position": "The following decree may follow from the truth/error contrast or from the people's being turned away.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports Zamakhshari's two connections; he also reports Ibn Atiyya comparing God's attributes with the people's chosen course."}, {"id": "10:32/q13/p2", "position": "God's prior decree explains why rebellious people will

{"id": "10:32/q15", "question": "Does God acquire judgments of good and bad from creatures?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:32/q15/p1", "position": "No. God originated creatures and cannot be affected by anything He made.", "reasons": "Al-Husayn is reported by Sulami."}]}
{"id": "10:32/q16", "question": "What fate of idols and worshippers is invoked in the surrounding argument?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:32/q16/p1", "position": "God gathers worshippers and idols, gives the idols life, then separates them as they disavow one another; each person receives good or evil's consequence.", "reasons": "Jishumi says manufactured deities cannot help, harm, avert punishment or independently intercede, reinforcing the verse's exclusive lordship."}]}
{"id": "10:32/q17", "question": "What is the verse taken to imply about playing chess and backgammon?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse and game reports prohibit play generally, or allow chess and confine the strongest prohibition to gambling.", "positions": [{"id": "10:32/q17/p1", "position": "These games are false or blameworthy and can be forbidden even without gambling.", "reasons": "Malik applies the verse to chess, backgammon and the game of fourteen, calling chess false and vain; Zuhri agrees. Qurtubi favors general prohibition as safer: Muslim transmits the pork-and-blood comparison for nardshir; Abu Musa's sound report calls nard disobedience; al-Halimi cites a chess disobedience report; Ali rebukes players for wasted life; Ibn Umar calls chess worse than nard; Abu Musa calls its players sinners; Abu Jafar calls it Zoroastrian. Qurtubi also cites a long report condemning players and spectators of backgammon, chess, walnuts and dice, with loss of good deeds, and notes their pairing with wine in al-Ma'ida. Al-Halimi says an authenticated report binds everyone. Ibn Umar stopped children's al-kajja; Ibn Abbas calls even that game gambling, while Ibn al-Arabi describes a rolled rag ball. Qurtubi rejects using Umar's war-model remark or companion silence as proof of idle play's permission. Al-Turtushi replies that chess misteaches warfare by moving the king away from capture."}, {"id": "10:32/q17/p2", "position": "Occasional private chess without gambling may be excused; nard reports might be restricted to gambling, and chess can be valued as an exercise of thought or warcraft.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports Maliki and majority allowance for occasional secret home play, and acknowledges that the nard prohibition might be limited to gambling by early permissions. Ibn al-Arabi reports Shafi'i reasoning that chess exercises thought, while chance-based backgammon resembles divining arrows; some Shafi'is even recommended chess after study in schools or mosques and ascribed it to early Muslims. Abu al-Fadl Ata al-Maqdisi says chess teaches warfare. Qurtubi rejects the claimed early attributions, mental benefit and the reading of Umar's remark as idle-play permission."}]}
{"id": "10:32/q18", "question": "When does play in chess or backgammon invalidate testimony?", "turns_on": "How habitual play, public reputation, gambling and general uprightness affect legal probity.", "positions": [{"id": "10:32/q18/p1", "position": "Habitual or public play damages probity and testimony; occasional private non-gambling chess is excused.", "reasons": "Malik doubts habitual players' testimony in Ibn Abi Hatim, Durr and Alusi; Qurtubi reports that Malikis and most jurists reject habitual public players because their reputation and probity fail, while excusing occasional secret home chess."}, {"id": "10:32/q18/p2", "position": "An otherwise upright player's testimony stands unless foolishness, suspicion, grave sin or gambling compromises probity.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports the Shafi'i school: gambling or becoming known for it invalidates probity through illicit wealth."}, {"id": "10:32/q18/p3", "position": "All these amusements are disliked, but a player with more good deeds than faults and no evident major sin retains acceptable testimony.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports Abu Hanifa's school, including chess, backgammon and the game of fourteen."}]}
{"id": "10:32/q19", "question": "What game names and materials are recorded?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "10:32/q19/p1", "position": "Chess and backgammon pieces are described as boxwood and elephant bone; backgammon also bears the names al-batil, al-ka'b, al-arn and nardshir.", "reasons": "Qurtubi supplies the materials and names."}]}
{"id": "100:1/q01", "question": "What does the opening wāw do?", "turns_on": "Whether the opening is a literal honorific oath, testimony, or a rhetorical evocation of an imagined scene.", "positions": [{"id": "100:1/q01/p1", "position": "It introduces God's oath by the chargers.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās says the oath wāw governs the genitive. Zayd b. Aslam declined to interpret the opening letters beyond calling them God's oath. Elmalılı calls it an oath. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ records the usual view that an oath magnifies its object, but criticizes the restrictive interpretations it produced. Islahi treats the oath as the animals' testimony to the later claim about ingratitude."}, {"id": "100:1/q01/p2", "position": "The wāw evokes the scene rhetorically rather than serving only as a literal oath.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ appeals to her treatment of 93:1 and says the honorific-oath assumption leaves the horse and camel dispute unresolved. Asad prefers an exclamatory rendering because the following clauses form an imagined parable."}, {"id": "100:1/q01/p3", "position": "It is an exclamation: 'Oh, the chargers!'", "reasons": "Asad prefers 'Oh' to his usual 'Consider' and most translators' 'By,' on the basis of the imaginary parable that follows."}]}
{"id": "100:1/q02", "question": "What does al-ʿādiyāt mean and how is it formed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "100:1/q02/p1", "position": "Swift runners or chargers, the feminine plural active participle of running.", "reasons": "Jishumī calls it the plural of ʿādiyah. Al-Qurṭubī defines running as rapid motion with limbs spread; Abū Ḥayyān says swift runners; al-Samīn and Bursevī explain the yāʾ replacing wāw after kasra, as does al-Ālūsī. Elmalılı traces ʿadw to crossing a limit: running, hostility, oppression, and spatial contagion are related senses; in battle ʿadī/ʿādiya name attacking troops, though some assign the former to infantry and the latter to cavalry. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the term especially describes horses and camels and can analogically describe human runners; he names al-Sulayk, al-Shanfarā, Taʾabbaṭa Sharran and ʿAmr b. Umayya. Its feminine form agrees with a non-rational referent."}]}
{"id": "100:1/q03", "question": "Who or what are the chargers?", "turns_on": "Whether ḍabḥ and the later sparks, dawn attack and dust fit horses or camels; the reported ʿAlī–Ibn ʿAbbās dispute and the number of horses at Badr; whether the oath may accommodate both or a further figurative referent.", "positions": [{"id": "100:1/q03/p1", "position": "Horses, usually cavalry charging or raiding in God's cause.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda and many others identify horses; some say the Prophet's cavalry, some a particular detachment, and some horses generally. Al-Ṭabarī chooses horses because camels do not pant; al-Rāzī adds that iron shoes spark and horses suit dawn attacks. Al-Ṭabrisī and others cite Ibn ʿAbbās's point that hooves raise dust. Al-Wāḥidī attributes preference to al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj. ʿAntarah and other poets depict panting chargers. Al-Ālūsī says Badr's few horses cannot exclude other horses or the delayed expedition, doubts the report and cites conflicting transmissions. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the five sequential descriptions favor a particular cavalry raid; Islahi says they fit warhorses but disputes confining them to Muslim raiders as the oath's moral proof. Ibn ʿAbbās, as reported by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, initially specified horses raiding for God's cause; al-Ṭabarī prefers horses because, in his judgment, camels do not make ḍabḥ."}, {"id": "100:1/q03/p2", "position": "Pilgrims' camels running from ʿArafāt through Muzdalifah to Minā.", "reasons": "ʿAlī invokes the one or two horses reported at Badr against identifying the oath with a cavalry raid; some versions name al-Miqdād alone, others him and al-Zubayr, and Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to recant. Ibn ʿAbbās's rival answer says the horses were a separate detachment. Ṣafiyyah's poem pictures animals at Jamʿ raising dust; Abū Ṣāliḥ and Muslim prefer ʿAlī's authority. Interpretations vary on whether the camels' ḍabḥ is breath, stretched necks or forelegs, or a metaphor; pilgrims kindle fires at Muzdalifah and raise dust en route, including Wādī Muḥassir. Al-Ṭabarī objects that camels do not pant; al-

Study Quran attributes to al-Bayḍāwī an allegory of souls conveying holiness, attaining knowledge and entering the highest Garden."}, {"id": "100:1/q03/p6", "position": "The image can extend to modern weapons and swift motorized assault vehicles.", "reasons": "Elmalılı relates fire-sparking arms and motor vehicles to the distinctive plurals and successive fāʾs as a historical development; on Meccan dating this would allude to equipment Muslims did not yet possess."}, {"id": "100:1/q03/p7", "position": "Camels, with no particular journey specified.", "reasons": "ʿAbd Allāh and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr identify the runners simply as camels; Ibrāhīm reports a camel interpretation and distinguishes camel breathing from horse panting."}]}
{"id": "100:1/q04", "question": "Do the horses denote a particular force or horses generally?", "turns_on": "Whether the definite article identifies the delayed expedition or names a general class, and whether the following actions describe one raid.", "positions": [{"id": "100:1/q04/p1", "position": "A particular expedition's horses are in view.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the definite article may refer to the expedition. {"id": "100:1/q05", "question": "What is ḍabḥ here?", "turns_on": "Whether ḍabḥ is a respiratory sound, a form of ḍabʿ describing gait, or a transferred term in the camel interpretation.", "positions": [{"id": "100:1/q05/p1", "position": "The hard runner's audible breath or panting, usually attributed to horses.", "reasons": "Authorities place the sound in the throat, chest, insides, mouth, nose or lips; al-Layth distinguishes it from neighing and Biqāʿī from snorting or bellowing. Ibn ʿAbbās imitates 'aḥ aḥ' or 'aj aj'; ʿAlī contrasts horse whinny-like panting with camel breath. Some call it snorting; al-Durr's version even has feet, whereas Ibn Mardawayh has nostrils. Exhaustion, fear and appetite may prompt it, and al-Qurṭubī suggests muzzles suppressed neighing lest an enemy be alerted. Al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Rāzī distinguish ordinary calls; Islahi says the breath reveals obedience and spent energy. ʿAntarah, an unnamed Iraqi poet and other poems illustrate charging horses. Ibrāhīm distinguishes camel breathing from a horse's panting; ʿAlī also distinguishes these sounds. ʿIkrimah describes the pant of a running horse."}, {"id": "100:1/q05/p2", "position": "It denotes vigorous running with stretched forelegs or necks, linked to ḍabʿ.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbaydah equates ḍabḥ and ḍabʿ; al-Azharī, al-Mubarrad and others describe extended forelegs, while some camel interpreters say stretched necks. Ṣafiyyah's poem is cited. Al-Kashshāf calls the letter substitution insecure; Ibn ʿĀshūr says linguists do not normally apply breath-sound ḍabḥ to camels and reports both dialect-substitution and metaphor alternatives; al-Qāmūs accepts interchange. Abū ʿUbaydah also allows the related verb for horses. Biqāʿī reports a nuance of running short of a full gallop. Al-Zamakhsharī reports an explanation in terms of camels' shoulders extending during travel, while saying its derivation is not established."}, {"id": "100:1/q05/p3", "position": "For camels it is a metaphorical application of the panting sound.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī conditions this on the authenticity of ʿAlī's report and likens it to transferred body terms; al-Samīn and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ repeat that analysis. Ibn ʿĀshūr also allows metaphor for a camel's intensified running sound. Al-Zamakhsharī compares metaphorical application to camels with bodily terms such as muzzle and hoof being transferred to humans, conditional on the report's soundness."}, {"id": "100:1/q05/p4", "position": "It is a rattling sound in the saddlebag or movement of the horses' lips.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī reports these two explanations from unnamed authorities; al-Naḥḥās has Ibn ʿAbbās describe blowing through the lips."}, {"id": "100:1/q05/p5", "position": "The word can also mean ash.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī records this lexical sense without applying it to the oath."}]}
{"id": "100:1/q06", "question": "Which creatures or things can make a ḍabḥ?", "turns_on": "Whether the reported restriction is sound and whether the wider Arabic examples are literal uses or metaphors.", "positions": [{"id": "100:1/q06/p1", "position": "Only horses and dogs, sometimes with foxes added, properly make the sound.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAṭāʾ and others give versions with dog and horse or with fox too; lexicographers are cited for the restricted list. Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and Biqāʿī say fox usage preceded transfer to horses; Tawbah's fox poem and the fire-darkening analogy support the usage. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī challenge the restriction as inconsistent with broader Arabic use. Al-Zamakhsharī reports a restriction to horses, dogs and foxes, alongside the horse and dog restriction attributed to ʿAṭāʾ and Ibn ʿAbbās."}, {"id": "100:1/q06/p2", "position": "Arabic usage extends ḍabḥ to many animals and even a bow or echo.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyyah lists camels, snakes, owls, rabbits, foxes, echoes and bows; Abū Ḥanīfah's poem gives a bow a fox-like ḍabḥ. Abū Ḥayyān doubts the restrictive Ibn ʿAbbās attribution. Al-Samīn regards wider uses as metaphors from a fox origin, whereas Ibn ʿAṭiyyah cites them against a strict animal limit.
